rationale: Zerah (2008) conducts a qualitative historical-institutional case study of Mumbai's water/sanitation and electricity sectors (supplemented by descriptive Census 2001 tabulations and secondary utility benchmarks) to test the splintering urbanism thesis. Multiple legal-institutional mechanisms are co-equally central empirical exposures: utility ownership and regulatory governance reforms (`regulatory_model_ownership`, including municipal monopoly vs private licensing, unbundling, corporatisation, ward-level delegated management contracts, and independent regulation) serve as the overarching analytical frame alongside tariff, ring-fenced cost-recovery, connection-fee, and cross-subsidy rules (`fees_tariffs_subsidies`), land-tenure and slum-notification service entitlements (`eligibility_status_documentation`), mandated CBO financial and operational participation in the Slum Sanitation Program (`participation_assistance`), complex connection procedures and mandatory licensed plumbers (`procedural_burden`), and metropolitan jurisdictional fragmentation (`institutional_structure_coordination`). Outcomes span household tap/sewerage/latrine network coverage (`primary_connection`, the primary water/sanitation metric in Table 2 and Section 3.2.1) alongside service intermittency, per-capita quantity, and shared vs in-premise service differentiation (`effective_access`) and household connection/tariff affordability (`economic_access`), warranting `multiple` for the multi-label outcome field.
